sections.description: Tap the sign that fits the rule.

sections.title: Overlaps and Matches
sections.description: Compare marks and measurements.

sections.title: Clue Checks
sections.description: Decide what the evidence supports.

questions.prompt: Tap the print trail showing a visitor that moved quickly.
questions.context: Invented field-guide rule for this mud strip: prints spaced more than 100 cm apart show quick movement. Closer spacing shows slower movement.
questions.explanation: Only the 140 cm trail exceeds the 100 cm threshold, so it is the quick mover. The other trails are all well under that spacing.

diagram.title: Mud strip, top view
diagram.description: Four schematic rectangles each show one trail of prints on a mud strip, labeled with the measured gap between prints.

questions.prompt: Tap the rub mark most consistent with a Ridge Elk antler rub.
questions.context: Invented rule: a Ridge Elk antler rub sits between 90 and 130 cm above the ground. The tree diagram shows four rub patches at the heights labeled.
questions.explanation: Only the patch at 110 cm falls inside the 90 to 130 cm band. The 165 cm, 60 cm and 15 cm patches are all outside it.

diagram.title: Tree trunk, side view
diagram.description: A schematic trunk with four rub patches stacked top to bottom. Higher on the diagram means higher above the ground.

questions.prompt: Which invented visitor most likely left this cone scene?
questions.context: Scene: a spruce cone stripped to its bare core, with its scales piled on a stump. Invented guide: Stump Chewer strips cones to the core and piles scales. Bark Finch pries scales but leaves the cone shape. Tunnel Mole ignores cones. Drift Hare nibbles buds only.
questions.explanation: A bare core with a scale pile matches the Stump Chewer entry. Bark Finch leaves the cone shape, and the others do not handle cones.

questions.prompt: Order the marks from earliest to latest using the overlaps.
questions.context: Invented sand patch. Strider prints lie under Hopper prints. Rain dimples sit on top of Hopper prints. Waddler prints cut across the rain dimples. A mark on top came later.
questions.explanation: Each overlap gives a before-and-after pair: Strider, then Hopper, then rain, then Waddler. Only one order satisfies all three overlaps.

items.label: Strider prints
Hopper prints
Rain dimples
Waddler prints

questions.prompt: Match each print description to the visitor it fits.
questions.context: Invented card. Reed Strider: unwebbed four-toe print, 12 cm long. Marsh Waddler: webbed four-toe print, 12 cm long. Dune Hopper: small paired prints, 5 cm long.
questions.explanation: Webbing separates Waddler from Strider at equal length, and small paired prints point to the Hopper. Two descriptions share the Waddler.

left.label: Paired 5 cm prints, 80 cm between pairs

questions.prompt: Classify each trail's pace using the spacing rule.
questions.context: Invented rule: gaps under 0.4 m mean slow, 0.4 m to 1.0 m mean steady, and gaps over 1.0 m mean fast. Convert units first.
questions.explanation: 20 cm is 0.2 m, so slow. 1.5 m is over 1.0 m, so fast. 60 cm is 0.6 m, so steady. Comparing needs matching units.

cells.label: Prints 20 cm apart
Prints 1.5 m apart
Prints 60 cm apart

questions.prompt: Tap the trail segment where the visitor paused.
questions.context: Invented rule: a walking visitor leaves prints one after another in alternating positions. A pause leaves two prints side by side at the same point on the trail.
questions.explanation: Side-by-side prints at one point show a pause. The alternating, single and angled segments all show continued movement or only one foot.

diagram.title: Trail, top view
diagram.description: A trail drawn left to right in four schematic segments, each describing the print pattern found there.

questions.prompt: Which direction does the evidence say the visitor traveled?
questions.context: Invented rule: toes point in the direction of travel. Five Reed Strider prints lie in a straight line, all with toes pointing toward the old fence to the west. The lake lies to the east.
questions.explanation: Toes show travel direction, so the visitor headed west toward the fence and away from the lake. Print length and count do not change that.

title: Season Reasoning Gauntlet
description: Reason through eight puzzles set on an invented planet to test whether orbit distance or axis tilt, day length and sun angle better explain seasons.

sections.title: Pick the better explanation
sections.description: Five claims about seasons on one invented planet.

sections.title: Match and test
sections.description: Link effects to causes and check claims against data.

questions.prompt: Veloria's orbit distance varies only 3%, but its axis is tilted. Which explanation better accounts for its seasons?
questions.context: Veloria is an invented planet. Its northern and southern halves have opposite seasons at the same moment, and the planet's distance from its star barely changes.
questions.explanation: Both halves are almost equally far from the star, yet their seasons differ. A tilt that makes one half lean toward the star and the other lean away explains this.

options.label: Veloria is closer to its star in summer, so distance drives the seasons
Tilt makes one half lean toward the star, changing day length and star angle
The star gets brighter in whichever half is warm
One half is always nearer the star than the other

questions.prompt: Compare the daily energy received by Town A and Town B. About how many times larger is A's total?
questions.context: Invented rule: daily energy equals sunlit hours times energy per hour. Town A has 14 sunlit hours at 0.8 units per hour. Town B has 10 sunlit hours at 0.5 units per hour.
questions.explanation: Town A gets 14 × 0.8 = 11.2 units; Town B gets 10 × 0.5 = 5 units. The ratio is about 2.2, combining longer days and steeper rays.

questions.prompt: At noon, a 1 m pole casts a 2 m shadow in Town P and a 0.5 m shadow in Town Q. Which town has the higher star?
questions.context: Invented rule: the higher the star is in the sky, the shorter a pole's shadow. Starlight arriving more directly spreads over less ground, so each patch of ground receives more energy.
questions.explanation: A shorter shadow means the star is higher. In Town Q the same starlight covers less ground area, so each patch heats up more.

options.label: Town Q, because its shadow is shorter
Town P, because its shadow is longer
Both, since the pole is the same height
Neither, since shadows only show day length

questions.prompt: Six months after Veloria's north leans toward its star, the planet is on the opposite side of its orbit. What is true?
questions.context: Veloria's axis always points toward the same distant star as the planet circles its own star. The axis does not flip or wobble.
questions.explanation: Because the axis keeps its direction while the planet moves around, the half that leaned away now leans toward the star. No flipping is needed.

options.label: The axis flips to the opposite direction
The planet wobbles so its tilt disappears
The north still leans toward the star
The axis keeps its direction, so the south now leans toward the star

questions.prompt: Imagine Veloria had no axis tilt but kept the same slightly oval orbit. What would happen to its tilt-driven seasons?
questions.context: Invented rule: a half that leans toward the star has longer days and a higher star. With no tilt, neither half ever leans toward or away from the star.
questions.explanation: Without tilt, no half leans toward the star, so day length stays near 12 hours year-round and the tilt-driven seasonal swing fades.

options.label: Seasons would grow stronger in both halves
Day length would stay close to 12 hours, and tilt-driven seasons would fade
One half would be stuck in permanent summer

questions.prompt: Match each observed effect on Veloria to its cause.
questions.context: Invented model: leaning toward the star lengthens days and raises the star's midday angle in that half. When one half leans toward the star, the other half leans away.
questions.explanation: Longer days and steeper rays both come from leaning toward the star. Opposite seasons arise because one half leans toward the star while the other leans away.

left.label: Higher midday star in that half
Opposite seasons in the two halves

right.label: The half leans toward the star
One half leans toward as the other leans away
A small change in orbit distance

questions.prompt: On the day Veloria's north leans most toward its star, match each town to its likely day length.
questions.context: Invented model: the leaning half gets about 15 hours of daylight, the other half gets about 9 hours, and the equator stays near 12 hours.
questions.explanation: The north leans toward the star, so it has long days. The south leans away and gets short days, while the equator hardly changes.

questions.prompt: Check each claim against Veloria's invented data table.
questions.context: Month 1: nearest the star, north 4°C, south 26°C. Month 7: farthest from the star, north 27°C, south 5°C. Temperatures are invented averages.
questions.explanation: Month 1 is nearest the star yet the north is cold, so distance alone fails. The halves swap, and the north peaks in the farthest month.

cells.label: Being nearest the star warms the whole planet
The warm and cold halves swap between the two months
The north's warmest month is the month farthest from the star

note: All puzzles use an invented planet called Veloria, with made-up temperatures and rules given in each question, so scoring depends only on the information supplied.

title: Follow the Drop
description: Trace raindrops through an invented mountain-to-sea watershed by ordering route steps, doing flow arithmetic, and matching coastal places to water-cycle processes.

questions.prompt: A raindrop lands on snow-covered ground. Order the steps it takes before reaching a stream.
questions.context: Simplified model: the drop stays frozen in the snow until it melts, then moves over the surface to a channel.
questions.explanation: The drop must melt before it can flow. Once liquid, it moves over the surface as runoff and then joins the stream.

items.label: Water joins a stream
The drop melts into liquid water
Meltwater runs across the surface

questions.prompt: On a gentle meadow, part of the meltwater soaks down into the soil. What is that process called?

questions.prompt: Order this drop's journey from the sea to the mountain soil.
questions.context: Simplified model: the drop begins in the ocean as liquid water and ends underground on a mountain slope.
questions.explanation: Liquid must evaporate to become vapor, vapor condenses into cloud droplets, rain falls, and only then can the drop infiltrate the soil.

items.label: The drop infiltrates mountain soil
Vapor condenses into cloud droplets
Ocean water evaporates
Rain falls on the mountain

questions.prompt: Using the invented Alder watershed map described, order the places a drop passes from Birch Creek to the sea.

questions.explanation: Each place flows into the next one in the supplied map, so the only valid route is creek, river, reservoir, estuary.

items.label: Pine Reservoir
Salt Estuary
Birch Creek
Larch River

questions.prompt: Match each coastal moment to the water-cycle process it shows.
questions.explanation: Warm sea water turning to vapor is evaporation, cooling vapor forming droplets is condensation, soaking into sand is infiltration, and flow over pavement is runoff.

left.label: Sun-warmed sea water turns to vapor
Rain streams across a paved harbor lot

questions.prompt: Match each seaside scene to its process. Some processes appear more than once.
questions.explanation: A drying puddle and drying towel lose liquid to vapor. Fog and dew form from vapor becoming liquid. Water draining through sand infiltrates, while rain off a seawall is runoff.

left.label: A puddle on the dock dries
Fog forms over a cold bay
Dew appears on a boat rail
Water drains down through a sandy beach
A wet towel dries on a line

questions.prompt: Two drops land on the same hillside. One soaks in and one flows downhill. What does this show about route maps?
questions.explanation: Water can take different paths depending on conditions such as soil and slope surface. A route map shows one possible path, not a guaranteed single route.

Water on land never enters the ground
Every drop must evaporate before reaching a stream

title: Pickles to Pond Osmosis
description: Predict which way water moves into or out of cells in salty brine, sugar syrup and fresh pond water, then match everyday examples to the process.

sections.title: Predict the Water
sections.description: Four cell scenarios

sections.title: Match and Reason
sections.description: Examples, processes and cause chains

questions.prompt: A cucumber slice sits in very salty water. What happens to its cells?
questions.context: Simplified model: a cell membrane lets water through but blocks dissolved solutes. Net water movement goes toward the side with more dissolved solute.

options.label: Water leaves the cells and they shrink
Water enters the cells and they swell
Salt flows in and the cells swell
Nothing moves because the cells are alive

questions.explanation: The brine has more dissolved solute than the cell contents, so water moves out toward it. The cells lose volume and the slice turns limp.

questions.prompt: A single-celled pond organism has more dissolved material inside than the fresh pond water around it. Which way does net water move?
questions.context: Use the same simplified model: water crosses the membrane, dissolved solutes do not.

options.label: Out of the cell into the pond
Into the cell from the pond
Solutes move out until the sides match

questions.explanation: Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, which is inside the cell. That is why pond organisms need ways to cope with constant water entry.

questions.prompt: Raisin cells are packed with dissolved sugars. What happens when raisins soak in plain water?
questions.context: Same simplified model. Sugar acts as a dissolved solute that cannot cross the membrane.

options.label: Water leaves the raisins and they shrivel more
Water enters the raisins and they plump up
Sugar leaves and the raisins stay the same size

questions.explanation: Inside the raisin cells the solute level is far higher than in plain water, so water moves in and the fruit swells.

questions.prompt: A cell holding 0.9 units of dissolved solute is placed in a solution also at 0.9 units. What is the net result?
questions.context: Same simplified model, with units measuring dissolved solute concentration on both sides of the membrane.

options.label: Water enters and the cell swells
Water leaves and the cell shrinks
Water enters for an hour, then leaves

questions.explanation: With equal solute levels on both sides, there is no concentration difference to drive net water movement. Individual water molecules still cross, but evenly in both directions.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the water movement that best describes it.
questions.context: Same simplified model: net water moves toward the side with more dissolved solute.

left.label: Cucumber slices sitting in strong brine
Cells in a solution matching their inner solute level

questions.explanation: Brine has more solute outside, so water leaves. Raisins have more inside, so water enters. Matching levels give no net movement.

questions.prompt: Match each case to the direction of net water movement, using the solute levels described.
questions.context: Salt or sugar counts as dissolved solute. Dry beans have far more solute inside than the soaking water. Pond water is fresh.

left.label: Salt sprinkled on eggplant slices, drawing out liquid
Pond protist cell in fresh pond water
Dry beans soaking in plain water

questions.explanation: Salt and sugar on the outside pull water out of the cells. Pond protists and soaking beans have more solute inside, so water moves in.

questions.prompt: Put the cause chain for a cucumber slice in brine in a valid order.
questions.context: Use cause and effect: each step must happen before the step it leads to.

items.label: Brine has more dissolved salt than the cell contents
Water moves out through the membrane
Cells lose volume and the slice turns limp
The slice is placed in the brine

questions.explanation: The slice must enter the brine first. The solute difference then drives water out, and the water loss is what shrinks the cells.

questions.prompt: A pond cell swollen from fresh water is moved into brine with more solute than its contents. What happens next?
questions.context: Same simplified model. The brine's solute level is higher than the cell's inner level.

options.label: Water keeps entering and the cell swells further
Water movement reverses and leaves the cell
Salt crosses in until nothing changes
Water stops and the cell stays swollen

questions.explanation: Direction depends on which side has more solute. Once the brine is saltier than the cell, net water flows out and the cell shrinks.

title: Freeze-Thaw Pothole Predictor

questions.prompt: Match each road water event to the water-cycle process it shows.
questions.context: Process meanings: infiltration means water enters the ground, runoff means water flows over the surface, and evaporation means liquid turns to gas.
questions.explanation: Water entering a crack goes below the surface (infiltration), water streaming to a drain is runoff, and a puddle turning to vapor is evaporation.

cells.label: Meltwater slips down into a crack and below the surface
Rain streams across the asphalt toward a storm drain
A warm afternoon turns a shallow puddle into invisible vapor

questions.prompt: Match each pavement event to the cause that produced it.
questions.context: Invented simplified model. Expansion pressure: ice takes up more room than the liquid water it came from. Lost support: thawing leaves an empty or soft space under the surface.
questions.explanation: Widening and lifting come from ice taking more room. A hollow left after melting removes support, so surfaces sink or break.

left.label: Frozen ridges lift a pavement edge
Thaw leaves a hollow beneath the surface
Wheels sink through a patch over a hollow

questions.prompt: For each situation, choose the next step the model predicts.
questions.context: Invented rules: freezing water widens a crack; melted ice leaves a void; wheels over a void can break loose pieces.
questions.explanation: Each step follows one rule: freezing widens, melting leaves a void, and loaded wheels over a void break pieces free.

cells.label: Water in a crack freezes overnight
Ice in the widened crack melts

options.label: The crack becomes narrower than before

cells.label: A loaded truck crosses a patch with a void

questions.prompt: Sort each observation under the road-damage ingredient it represents.
questions.context: Invented model ingredients: water supply puts liquid in cracks, temperature swing crosses freezing, traffic load presses on weakened pavement.
questions.explanation: Snowmelt and rain supply water, crossing freezing back and forth is a temperature swing, and trucks and buses add load.

left.label: Two freezes and two thaws in one week

questions.prompt: Put the invented pothole chain in an order that respects its dependencies.
questions.context: Rules: ice needs water in the crack first, melting follows ice, and wheels break pieces only after a void exists.
questions.explanation: Water must arrive before ice, melting must follow ice, a void must exist before wheels break pieces, and the pothole opens last.

items.label: Water enters the crack
Ice forms and widens the crack
Ice melts, leaving a void
Wheels break the weakened patch
Loose pieces leave an open pothole

questions.explanation: Water that widens a crack must have frozen, an unsupported surface is crushed by wheels, and ejected pieces enlarge the pothole.

cells.label: Water enters, then ?, then the crack widens
Ice melts, a void forms, then ?
Wheels pound loose pieces, pieces fly out, then ?

questions.explanation: Damage needs water, then freezing, then thawing, then traffic. Missing any one stage stops the chain at that point.

cells.label: Dry crack, night -3 °C, day 4 °C

Water stays liquid, so no freezing damage

title: Predict, Reveal, Revise
description: Make three provisional predictions, then read new labeled results and choose which explanation the completed evidence still supports.

sections.title: Predict
sections.description: Commit to a first guess. These are not scored.

sections.title: Reveal
sections.description: Read the results and pick the supported conclusion.

sections.title: Revise
sections.description: One follow-up result, based on your first prediction.

questions.prompt: Make a provisional prediction: what most likely drives the seedlings' tilt?
questions.context: Invented experiment: a tray of seedlings tilts toward a window. The window side is both brighter and slightly warmer than the far side of the room.
questions.explanation: Both ideas fit this first observation, so a guess is reasonable. The next reveal tests them separately.

questions.prompt: Make a provisional prediction: why does a crescent Moon look like a crescent?
questions.context: A crescent Moon is seen after sunset. Explanation A: Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon. Explanation B: we see only part of the Moon's sunlit half.
questions.explanation: Both explanations match a crescent shape at first glance. The reveal adds a labeled model result to separate them.

options.label: Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon
We see only part of the sunlit half

questions.prompt: Make a provisional prediction: where did the puddle's water go?
questions.context: Invented backyard case: a shallow puddle on a flat, sealed patio shrinks to nothing over a sunny afternoon.
questions.explanation: Hidden drainage and vapor both fit a vanishing puddle. The reveal supplies a controlled comparison.

options.label: It drained away through hidden cracks
It changed from liquid to vapor

questions.prompt: Which explanation of the seedling tilt remains supported by this dataset?
questions.context: Reveal, invented lab data. Tray 1: a cool LED on the left, a dark heating pad on the right, all else equal. After three days seedlings tilt a mean 18° left. Tray 2 (control): no LED, no pad; mean tilt 0°.
questions.explanation: The tilt followed the LED, not the warm pad on the opposite side, and the control stayed upright. Attraction to warmth is not supported here.

options.label: Seedlings tilt toward the brighter light; warmth attraction fails
Seedlings tilt toward the warmer side
The tilt is random, since a control exists

questions.prompt: Which explanation of Moon phases does this model result support?
questions.context: Reveal, classroom model. One lamp lights a foam ball. Walking around the ball, you see a lit part that changes from thin crescent to full. Your head's shadow touches the ball only when your head is exactly in line between lamp and ball.
questions.explanation: The changing view of one lit half explains the phases. Earth's shadow on the Moon is a separate event, a lunar eclipse.

options.label: Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon
We view different amounts of the sunlit half
The light source changes its shape
The ball itself changes its shape

questions.prompt: Choose the water-cycle process that explains each tray result.
questions.context: Reveal, invented trays. Both trays are watertight, with no holes and no spills. Tray A has no lid and is open to the air: its water level falls 8 mm in six hours. Tray B has a clear lid that stays cooler than the water: its level falls 1 mm, and droplets bead on the lid's underside.
questions.explanation: With no holes or spills, water in Tray A could only leave as vapor (evaporation). Vapor meeting Tray B's cooler lid turned back into liquid droplets (condensation).

cells.label: Tray A's falling water level
Droplets under Tray B's lid

questions.prompt: If you predicted light, what does this added dataset support?
questions.context: Invented follow-up, no heater used. Three trays each, LED on the left. Dim LED: mean tilt 6°. Bright LED: mean tilt 19°.
questions.explanation: Brighter light gave a larger tilt in these trays, and dim light still produced some tilt. No warmth was involved, so it cannot explain the difference.

options.label: Brighter light produced a larger tilt in these trays
Extra warmth caused the larger tilt
Tilt does not depend on brightness

questions.prompt: If you predicted warmth, what does this heater-only result support?
questions.context: Invented follow-up. Tray with the heating pad on the right at 30°C, no LED, all else equal: mean tilt 1°. The earlier cool-LED tray tilted 18°.
questions.explanation: Warmth alone produced almost no tilt, while a cool LED produced a large one. Revising a first prediction after evidence is good science.

options.label: Warmth alone did not produce the tilt seen with the LED
The heater produced a large tilt
Warmth and light are both required together
The heater result says nothing about the cause

title: Spot the Weak Science Claim
description: Read short invented headlines, pick the claim that outruns its evidence, match weak spots to the evidence that would help, then order the steps of a fair test.

questions.prompt: Which part of this headline goes furthest beyond what the small study can show?
questions.context: Invented headline: 'Study proves tea cures sleepiness.' In the invented study, 12 volunteers drank tea and 9 said they felt less sleepy afterward. There was no comparison group.

options.label: Tea 'proves' and 'cures' sleepiness for people in general

questions.explanation: Twelve people with no comparison group can suggest a pattern, but cannot prove a cure for everyone. The strong causal words are the overreach.

questions.prompt: Which sentence goes beyond the evidence in this invented moss-walk result?
questions.context: Invented data: 40 students who chose to join a weekend moss-walk club scored higher on a quiz than 40 students who did not join.

options.label: Club members scored higher on this quiz than non-members.
Both groups took the same quiz.

questions.explanation: Students chose the club themselves, so other differences could explain the scores. A single quiz also does not measure overall smartness.

questions.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by this invented greenhouse note?
questions.context: Invented note: Five bean plants given Gro-Max fertilizer in one greenhouse grew taller than the five plants grown there last year.

options.label: Gro-Max boosts growth of crops all over the world.
The comparison plants came from last year.
The plants grew in a single greenhouse.

questions.explanation: Five bean plants in one greenhouse say nothing reliable about every crop in every place. The other statements only restate what was done.

questions.prompt: The headline 'Telescopes improve sleep' rests on owners sleeping better. Which point shows its cause might be wrong?
questions.context: Invented survey: in a made-up town, telescope owners reported better sleep than non-owners.

options.label: Well-rested people may have more energy for stargazing, so the cause could run the other way.
Telescope owners were the people asked about their sleep.
The headline is only four words long.
Sleep can be counted in hours.

questions.explanation: A link between two things does not show which causes which. Good sleep might lead to the hobby, rather than the telescope leading to good sleep.

questions.prompt: Match each weak spot in this invented paint claim to the evidence that would help most.
questions.context: Invented headline: 'Glow-Pebble paint cuts classroom mold.' Six rooms in one school were painted and compared only with their own earlier counts.

left.label: Rooms were compared only with their own earlier counts
Only six rooms in one school were tested
One person judged mold by a quick glance

right.label: Unpainted rooms checked over the same period
A consistent counting method for mold

questions.explanation: Unpainted rooms show what changes anyway, more sites show whether it generalizes, and a fixed counting method makes results comparable.

questions.prompt: Match each weak spot in this invented playlist claim to the evidence that would help most.
questions.context: Invented headline: 'Brainwave Beats playlist boosts memory.' Students knew which group got the playlist, the playlist's creator ran the study, and the groups took different quizzes.

left.label: Students knew they had the playlist and expected a boost
Only the playlist's creator ran the study

right.label: A look-alike silent track, with students unaware which they get
A repeat of the study by an independent team
The identical quiz given to every group
More students from the same single class

questions.explanation: Hidden group assignment limits expectation effects, independent repeats limit bias, and one shared quiz makes the scores comparable.

questions.prompt: Match each weak spot in this invented town claim to the evidence that would help most.
questions.context: Invented headline: 'Marlow bike lanes cause fewer shop closures.' Marlow was compared with one other town, only surviving shops were counted, and only one year after the lanes was studied.

left.label: Marlow was compared with just one other town
Only shops still open were counted
Only one year after the lanes was studied

right.label: Records of every shop, including ones that closed
Several comparison towns without new lanes
Data across many years, before and after

questions.explanation: Ignoring closed shops hides the very outcome under study. Extra towns and extra years show whether Marlow's result is unusual or lasting.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of a fair lamp-schedule test so every stated rule holds.
questions.context: Invented greenhouse test of a new lamp schedule. Rules: groups are split before anyone gets the schedule; the schedule and the chosen measuring method both come before final measuring; the comparison comes last.

items.label: Decide how seedling height will be measured
Split the seedlings randomly into two groups
Give only one group the new lamp schedule
Measure all seedlings after four weeks
Compare the two groups' results

questions.explanation: Random splitting must precede treatment, and measuring needs both the treatment and a fixed method. Deciding the method and splitting are independent, so either may come first.

title: Citizen Science Team Builder
description: Work together on an invented backyard bird-count team: assign roles from stated needs, sequence a weekly session, and decide which records to trust.

sections.title: Build the roles
sections.description: Match people, steps and rules to a weekly count.

sections.title: Check the data
sections.description: Decide which records the team can trust.

questions.prompt: Give each invented team member the one role their stated equipment allows.
questions.context: Roles: Timekeeper needs a working watch. Counter needs binoculars. Typist needs a home laptop. Species checker needs a field guide. Each person has exactly one of these items and the team has four roles.
questions.explanation: Roles follow what each task requires, not guesses about people. Each item fits one role, so the assignment is unique.

questions.prompt: The team counts backyard birds weekly. Why must the recorder note the time and place of each count?

options.label: Bird numbers change with time of day and spot, so counts only compare fairly when both are known.
It makes the spreadsheet look longer and more official.
It lets the team average all counts into one daily number.
It proves the birds stayed in the same place all week.

questions.explanation: Context lets later readers compare like with like. A count at dawn in a park and one at noon in a yard answer different questions.

questions.prompt: Arrange the weekly session steps so every dependency is respected.
questions.context: The team needs: the count window agreed before counting, the start time and spot recorded before counting, and the sheet typed up only after counting ends.

items.label: Agree on a 10-minute count window
Record start time and spot name
Count birds during the window
Type the sheet into the shared file

questions.explanation: Counting depends on both setup steps, and typing depends on counting. The two setup steps are independent, so either order works.

questions.prompt: Apply the team's counting rules to each situation and choose what goes on the sheet.
questions.context: Rules: for each species record the most birds seen together at one moment; never add repeat sightings. Birds you cannot identify are logged as Unknown, never guessed.

cells.label: 3 sparrows at the start, later 5 sparrows together
One robin leaves and returns, seen one at a time
A call from a hidden bird nobody can name

questions.explanation: The max-together rule avoids double counting, and honest Unknown entries keep guesses out of the data.

questions.prompt: Three finch records arrived. Which one should the team trust most for comparing weeks?
questions.context: Record A: 12 finches, no time or place. Record B: 9 finches, 8:00 to 8:10, Maple Park north gate, counted by Jun in the agreed window. Record C: 20 finches, copied from last week's sheet.
questions.explanation: Record B has time, place, observer and method. A lacks context and C is not a new observation.

questions.prompt: Priya typed 14 sparrows, but the paper sheet says 4. What should the team do?
questions.context: Team rule: never erase an original entry. Corrections are added as new, labeled lines.

options.label: Keep both and add a correction line citing the paper sheet's 4

questions.explanation: The paper sheet is the original observation. A labeled correction keeps the trail visible without losing the typing error.

questions.prompt: Which location note may go in the shared file under the team's privacy rule?
questions.context: Team rule: record only general public spot names. Never record home or school addresses, or photos of children.

options.label: 14 Larch Street, the Mateo family home
Back gate of Westfield Elementary at 3:15
Photo of Priya's nephew pointing at a nest

questions.explanation: A general public spot keeps the data usable and protects people. The other three break the stated privacy rule.

questions.prompt: Connect each checklist item to every member whose stated duty covers it.
questions.context: Mateo: write the start time and spot name. Amara: read her tally aloud. Jun: confirm species names with the field guide. Priya: type the sheet and compare each typed number with Amara's read tally.
questions.explanation: The count comparison needs Amara's read tally and Priya's check. Each other item is covered by one stated duty.

title: Mineral Scratch Lab
description: Learn what hardness means for minerals and how the Mohs scale orders them, then read invented scratch logs to rank samples by the lab's own toy rules.

questions.prompt: In the Mohs scale, what does a mineral's hardness describe?

options.label: How heavy it is for its size
How easily it splits into flat pieces

questions.explanation: USGS describes hardness as a mineral's resistance to scratching. Weight, shine and splitting are different properties.

questions.prompt: Order these minerals from least to most resistant to scratching on the Mohs scale.

items.label: Calcite
Quartz
Talc
Diamond
Fluorite

questions.explanation: The scale runs talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, feldspar 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, sapphire 9, diamond 10. So these five go talc, calcite, fluorite, quartz, diamond.

questions.prompt: Match each mineral to its place on the Mohs scale.
questions.context: Two of the numbers on the right belong to minerals that are not on the left and will stay unused.
questions.explanation: Talc is 1, fluorite 4, feldspar 6 and sapphire 9. The unused 5 is apatite and the unused 10 is diamond.

questions.prompt: What do the numbers 1 to 10 on the Mohs scale tell you?
questions.context: The Mohs scale is a qualitative ranking: a mineral with a higher number scratches one with a lower number. Its numbers are not equal units.

options.label: A mineral rated 6 is exactly twice as scratch resistant as one rated 3
They give a relative order of scratch resistance; the steps are not equal amounts
Each step up the scale adds the same amount of scratch resistance
A higher number means the mineral can never break

questions.explanation: The scale ranks minerals by which can scratch which. It is an order, not a measurement, so a 6 is not twice a 3. Hardness does not measure toughness or how easily a sample breaks.

questions.prompt: Judge each statement against the invented scratch log.
questions.context: Lab rules (toy): if Sample X leaves a scratch on Sample Y, X is harder than Y. If X is tried on Y and leaves no scratch, X is not harder than Y, so X is softer or equal. If X and Y are each tried on the other and neither scratches, treat them as equally hard. Harder-than carries through a chain: if X is harder than Y and Y is harder than Z, X is harder than Z. Samples treated as equally hard compare the same way to every other sample. Log: 1. A scratches B. 2. B scratches C. 3. C and D are each tried on the other and neither scratches. 4. C scratches E. 5. F scratches E.

cells.label: A is harder than C.

options.label: Cannot be told from the log

cells.label: D is harder than E.

options.label: Cannot be told from the log

cells.label: E is harder than B.

options.label: Cannot be told from the log

cells.label: C and D are equally hard.

options.label: Cannot be told from the log

cells.label: F is harder than C.

options.label: Cannot be told from the log

cells.label: C is harder than A.

options.label: Cannot be told from the log

questions.explanation: The scratches give A harder than B, B harder than C and C harder than E. C and D scratched neither way, so they are equal and D is also harder than E. F beats only E, so its rank against C is unknown. E is softer than B, and C is softer than A.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from the one trial in this log?
questions.context: Lab rules (toy): if Sample X leaves a scratch on Sample Y, X is harder than Y. If X is tried on Y and leaves no scratch, X is not harder than Y, so X is softer or equal. Log: Sample G was tried on Sample H and left no scratch. Nobody tried H on G.

options.label: G is softer than H, or equally hard
G and H are equally hard

questions.explanation: A failed scratch only shows that G is not harder. It cannot separate softer from equal. Trying H on G would settle which.

questions.prompt: Two unlabeled stones each scratch calcite, and quartz scratches each of them. What is supported?
questions.context: Calcite is 3 and quartz is 7 on the Mohs scale. Stone 1 and Stone 2 are invented samples. A scratch means the scratcher is harder.

options.label: Both are harder than calcite and softer than quartz, but hardness alone does not show they are the same mineral
They must be the same mineral
Both are exactly 5 on the Mohs scale

questions.explanation: Scratching calcite puts each above 3 and being scratched by quartz puts each below 7. Fluorite (4), apatite (5) and feldspar (6) all fall in that range, so hardness alone cannot show the two stones are the same mineral.

questions.prompt: Rank the five invented samples from hardest to softest using the trials.
questions.context: Lab rules (toy): if Sample X leaves a scratch on Sample Y, X is harder than Y. If X is tried on Y and leaves no scratch, X is not harder than Y. Trials: S scratches R. R scratches P. P scratches Q. Q scratches T. T was tried on S and left no scratch.

items.label: Sample P
Sample Q
Sample R
Sample S
Sample T

questions.explanation: The four scratches form a chain: S, then R, then P, then Q, then T. The failed trial of T on S agrees, since it only says T is not harder than S.

sources.label: USGS: Natural Gemstones, mineral hardness and the Mohs scale
USGS: Jaggar (1950), Abrasion hardness

note: The scratch logs, samples and lab rules are invented for practice, and the scale facts come from the USGS reference. This is not a field identification tool or a physical experiment, so do not try to scratch real specimens based on it.

title: Bats Beyond the Vampire Myth
description: Meet a ground-listening hunter, a cactus pollinator and food-sharing vampire bats. Eight discoveries replace a single spooky stereotype with different animals and ways of life.

questions.prompt: A bat uses echoes while flying at night. Which claim about its eyes should you reject?
questions.explanation: Bats are not blind. Echolocation does not replace eyes with an absence of vision; sensory use varies among species.

options.label: Using echolocation means the animal is blind
Vision and echolocation can both help a bat
Bats have eyes as well as other senses

questions.prompt: A pallid bat is hunting something moving on the ground. What helps it locate that prey?
questions.explanation: Pallid bats listen for prey-generated sounds. The White Sands account distinguishes that passive listening from echolocation used for orientation and avoiding obstacles.

options.label: Echoes from calls aimed at the prey
Sounds made by the prey itself
Vibrations detected through its feet while perched

questions.prompt: Put this lesser long-nosed bat's flower visit in a causal sequence.
questions.explanation: The bat feeds, picks up pollen, and carries it to another flower. A nectar meal can also move pollen between plants.

items.label: Pollen on the bat reaches another flower during a later visit
The bat reaches into a flower to drink nectar
Its head picks up pollen while feeding

questions.prompt: In Carter and colleagues' study, what tended to precede new food-sharing between unfamiliar female common vampire bats?
questions.explanation: The study followed introduced female common vampire bats in captivity. Increasing reciprocal grooming preceded first food donations; it does not establish a rule for every bat or for human friendships.

options.label: A growing similarity in contact calls

questions.prompt: After a lesser long-nosed bat eats cactus fruit, what can happen to the seeds?
questions.explanation: The NPS account describes seeds passing through intact. Fruit eating and pollination are different ways bats can help plants.

options.label: They are all digested along with the pulp
Some pass through intact, helping disperse the plant
They are carried to the next flower in the bat's cheeks

questions.prompt: Which additional use of lesser long-nosed bats’ day roosts does the cited NPS account specifically describe?
questions.explanation: Day roosts can also be maternity sites. The NPS account describes repeated use of suitable refuges, making the roost part of the bats' life cycle.

options.label: Maternity sites where bats give birth and raise pups
Winter hibernation sites for the whole colony
Mating territories held by individual males

questions.prompt: In its Saguaro account, which other animal’s former home does the NPS say can shelter big brown bats?
questions.explanation: The Saguaro account records big brown bats roosting in woodpecker holes as well as human-made structures. One animal's former cavity can become another animal's shelter.

options.label: A kangaroo-rat burrow beneath the soil
A woodpecker hole in a saguaro

questions.prompt: These bats do not all have the same dinner. Match each to the food described in the park accounts.
questions.explanation: Big brown bats eat many beetles; Mexican long-tongued bats feed on nectar and pollen; pallid bats take ground-dwelling arthropods including scorpions. Common names are clues to different lives, not Latin-name test questions.

right.label: A diet described as mostly beetles

National Park Service: pallid bat at White Sands

note: Species and study limits matter. The grooming finding concerns unfamiliar female common vampire bats in a captive study. This quiz gives no animal-handling or health advice.

title: Eight Lights in the Dark
description: Blue surf, rainbow combs, luminous wood and a predator’s private searchlight: discover eight reasons the natural world can look otherworldly. Some creatures make light; others transform light arriving from outside.

questions.prompt: In the May 2018 San Diego display reported by Scripps, what made breaking waves flash blue at night?
questions.explanation: Movement stimulated light from the bloom’s bioluminescent dinoflagellates. The report concerns May 2018; it explicitly says some red tides do not glow.

options.label: Moonlight reflected by red pigments in the water
Chemical light from dinoflagellates disturbed by water movement
A blue pigment released when seaweed broke apart

questions.prompt: A comb jelly’s comb rows shimmer in rainbow colours under white external light. What produces that particular rainbow?
questions.explanation: The moving combs diffract incoming light. Many comb jellies also produce their own light, but that is distinct from the rainbow seen under external illumination.

options.label: The comb rows split incoming light by diffraction
The animal mixes several colours of chemical light along each row
Pigments in the combs store white light and release it later

questions.prompt: A firefly courtship exchange is a conversation in light. Choose the best interpretation of each change.
questions.explanation: In flashing species, patterns help potential mates recognise each other. Bright artificial light can interfere with that exchange. These are communication functions, not evidence that every flash results in mating.

cells.label: An adult male produces his species’ courtship flash pattern

options.label: A signal that can help a female recognise a potential mate
A beam used mainly to illuminate the path ahead
Evidence that a female has already accepted him

cells.label: A bright flashlight is directed into the ongoing exchange

options.label: It necessarily makes the signal easier to recognise
It can disrupt the light-based communication
It supplies the energy the beetles need to make their flashes

questions.prompt: A piece of decaying wood shows the faint light called foxfire, even without a lamp shining on it. What is doing the light-making?
questions.explanation: Foxfire is living fungal light. The Missouri account describes luminous wood-decaying fungi, including light from honey-mushroom mycelium; the wood itself is not a little fire.

options.label: Mineral crystals reflecting starlight through the wood
Heat left over from the wood’s decay
Bioluminescent fungi living in the wood

questions.prompt: A scorpion appears blue-green under ultraviolet light. What happens to the energy in this fluorescence?
questions.explanation: Fluorescence transforms incoming light; bioluminescence generates light chemically. The museum locates the scorpion effect in the outer covering. The glow’s biological purpose remains debated.

options.label: The shell absorbs incoming ultraviolet light and emits visible light
The scorpion burns stored food to power a firefly-like lantern
Its shell simply reflects the ultraviolet light without changing it

questions.prompt: Who actually produces the light inside the lure of the deep-sea anglerfish described by Smithsonian Ocean?
questions.explanation: Bacteria supply the lure’s glow. The fish positions that light near its mouth to attract prey: the animal using the signal is not necessarily the organism making it.

options.label: Microscopic algae living inside the lure
Luminous bacteria living in the lure
The fish’s own cells, without a microbial partner

questions.prompt: How can a squid make itself harder to see by switching on lights? Order the counterillumination chain.
questions.explanation: An upward-looking hunter can detect a dark outline against brighter water. Matching that background with light from the underside reduces the contrast. This is camouflage, not a general guarantee of invisibility.

items.label: The contrast between squid and background becomes smaller
An unlit squid forms a dark outline against light arriving from above
A hunter below has a less distinct outline to detect
The squid emits belly light that matches the overhead background

questions.prompt: Some dragonfish can both emit and detect far-red light. Why can that combination help them hunt?
questions.explanation: The advantage depends on the difference between the fish’s vision and that of nearby animals. Its red light has limited range, but can illuminate prey without alerting animals unable to detect it.

options.label: Red light travels farther through seawater than blue light
Far-red light makes every nearby animal glow visibly
Many nearby animals cannot see the light illuminating them

title: NASA’s Spooky October Sky, Explained
description: Read eight original text descriptions of NASA and Chandra images, then discover what the eerie shapes actually record: active regions, reflected starlight, gas emissions, a young star’s shadow, and more. Every observation is historical or archival; nothing here promises what is visible tonight.

sources.label: NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory: Pumpkin Sun (October 8, 2014 image)
NASA Night Sky Network: October’s Night Sky Notes: Spooky Stargazing (September 28, 2026)
NASA Hubble: The Ghost Head Nebula (NGC 2080)
NASA Hubble: Serpens Nebula, HBC 672
NASA Hubble image record: Ghost of Cassiopeia / IC 63
Chandra 2023 MSH 15-52 release: Chandra/IXPE X-rays and DECaPS2 infrared survey data
NASA Hubble image record: CW Leonis, observations in 2011 and 2016; released October 28, 2021

note: The quiz uses text descriptions and links to dated NASA/Chandra records; it does not display or reproduce the images. Colorized astronomical images are not necessarily views in ordinary visible light. No current sky visibility or event timing is claimed.

questions.prompt: NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory recorded an October 8, 2014 Sun image that resembles a jack-o’-lantern. What are the bright patches actually marking?
questions.context: NASA’s record says the image combines ultraviolet wavelengths, which are colorized for display.
questions.explanation: The brighter regions trace active areas associated with intense, complex magnetic fields in the Sun’s corona. The pumpkin face is a visual resemblance in an ultraviolet image, not a visible-light photograph of a surface carving.

options.label: Flames burning on the Sun’s visible surface
Solar active regions linked to magnetic fields in the corona
Dark holes cut into the Sun to make a face
The silhouettes of planets crossing the Sun together

questions.prompt: Why can the faint Witch Head outline be seen in NASA’s account of IC 2118?
questions.context: The cloud contains dust near the bright star Rigel. It is too faint to be an easy naked-eye target, and the described dust is not a solid glowing surface.
questions.explanation: IC 2118 is a reflection nebula: dust scatters light from nearby Rigel. The cue is the cloud’s dust beside a bright star, not its spooky name.

options.label: The dust burns steadily like a tiny star
Sunlight bounces off a solid face-shaped object
Brief electrical flashes keep drawing its outline
Its dust scatters light from nearby Rigel

questions.prompt: The Ghost Head’s two eye-like patches are different. Which physical reading fits each one?
questions.context: In the enhanced-color Hubble record, A1 has a rounded bubble in glowing gas. A2 looks more complex and dustier. Massive young stars can drive radiation and particle winds; dust can partly conceal stars.

cells.label: The rounded A1 bubble suggests…

options.label: a solid planet making a dark silhouette
a massive star clearing surrounding gas with radiation and wind

cells.label: The dustier A2 patch could contain…

options.label: several massive stars partly hidden by dust
only an empty cavity with no stars

questions.explanation: NASA attributes A1’s bubble to one massive star’s radiation and wind. Dust makes A2 more complex and conceals several massive stars. The red, blue, and green of the wider nebula encode hydrogen and oxygen emission, not surface paint.

questions.prompt: HBC 672’s Bat Shadow spans a huge region of cloud, although the structure casting it is too small for Hubble to resolve directly. Which conclusion about size follows?
questions.context: NASA identifies the dark wings as a shadow projected onto the young star’s surrounding cloud. The pattern and the material casting it are in different places.
questions.explanation: The disk near HBC 672 is unresolved, but its shadow spreads across the birth cloud. A large projected pattern can reveal a small hidden structure; the shadow’s span is not the disk’s physical diameter.

options.label: The dark span measures a projected pattern on the cloud, not the physical width of the material near the star
The dark span directly measures the full physical width of the material around the star
The casting material must be at least as wide as every part of its shadow
Seeing the shadow means Hubble has also resolved the material itself

questions.prompt: What physical relationship best explains IC 63’s bright edge and ghostly veil?
questions.context: In Hubble’s archived record, the cloud of gas and dust lies close to the blue giant Gamma Cassiopeiae. The edge facing that star is bright; a veil extends away. The star itself is outside this Hubble frame.

options.label: Earth’s gravity draws the distant cloud into a tail
A solid body has punched the veil out of the cloud
Energy from Gamma Cassiopeiae excites and shapes nearby gas and dust
The shape is a trail left by Hubble’s camera motion

questions.explanation: NASA attributes the red hydrogen glow to ultraviolet radiation from Gamma Cassiopeiae and the blue to its light reflected by dust. The star’s influence explains the bright edge and flowing shape.

questions.prompt: Use the physical clues to connect the ghostly hand’s features with their astronomical roles.
questions.context: A pulsar is a compact spinning star whose continuing particle outflow can form a wind nebula. In this image, the small source near the palm’s base feeds the extended hand. A separate cloud beyond the fingertips is older debris from the explosion that left the compact source.
questions.explanation: The palm-base spot is the pulsar; its energetic particle wind shapes the hand-like nebula; and the low-energy X-ray clouds beyond the fingertips belong to the surrounding supernova remains. Chandra’s main release attributes the infrared layer to DECaPS2.

left.label: Blobby spot near the palm’s base
Mottled cloud just beyond the fingertips

right.label: Cloud from the supernova that created the pulsar

questions.prompt: How can Algol’s regular dimming and brightening happen from our viewpoint?
questions.context: NASA describes an orbiting pair in Algol’s triple-star system. Their alignment sometimes places one star in front of the other as viewed from Earth.

items.label: The two stars continue around their shared orbit
One moves in front of the other from Earth’s viewpoint
The pair’s combined light appears dimmer
As the alignment passes, the combined light brightens again

questions.explanation: An eclipse is a temporary alignment during an orbit: overlap reduces the light we receive, and the light rises after the stars separate in our view. TESS records the cycle; the telescope does not cause it.

questions.prompt: Which reading of CW Leonis keeps the observed arcs separate from the still-unsettled beams?
questions.context: Hubble’s records show expanding orange-red arcs around an aging carbon star and beams whose brightness changed across years. Its outer layers spread into an uneven envelope; astronomers have not pinned down why the beams changed.

options.label: Both arcs and beam changes have a single proven cause: a fixed opening in the dust
The arcs are expelled carbon-rich dust; openings in that dust may let some starlight through
The arcs are planetary orbits; the beams are planets crossing the star
Both features are only the boundaries of Hubble’s color filters

questions.explanation: Ejected carbon-rich dust makes the arcs. NASA treats gaps as a possible way for starlight beams to emerge, while the cause of their brightness changes remains unresolved.

title: A Pumpkin, from Flower to Next Seed
description: Follow a pumpkin from two different flowers to the carved fruit and seeds for a later generation. Apply qualified Extension and USDA clues without relying on an unseen plant image.

Illinois Extension, Pumpkin Varieties
USDA ARS, Squash Production
University of Minnesota Extension, Fruits and Vegetables That Require Pollination
Illinois Extension, Why Are My Pumpkin Fruit Dying After Bloom?
Original text-only pumpkin cases and comparisons; no botanical image or schematic is displayed.
Clemson Cooperative Extension, Pumpkins: Fruit or Veggie? (botanical definition, 2024)

note: All botany is text based and qualified. No plant diagram, universal colour rule, or garden diagnosis is implied.

questions.prompt: A pumpkin vine bears flowers. Why can the carved pumpkin be called a fruit in botany?
questions.context: Ignore where a food appears on a menu; classify the plant structure.

options.label: It develops from a flower’s ovary and holds seeds
It grows from a swollen root below the vine
It is a modified leaf that protects the flowers

questions.explanation: The fruit develops from the flower’s ovary and contains seeds; culinary use is a separate convention.

questions.prompt: A grower wants to mark a blossom that could develop into a pumpkin. Which observation should guide the tag?
questions.context: USDA describes female Cucurbita flowers as having a small squash-like structure below the petals; male flowers have a straight stem. Cards describe unseen flowers, not drawn images.

options.label: Card A: petals above a straight, narrow stem
Card B: petals above a rounded base that joins the vine
Card C: petals with a dark stripe but no base recorded

questions.explanation: The rounded base on B fits the described ovary beneath a female flower. Petal colour alone would not establish that structure.

questions.prompt: If one part of a successful pollination path were missing, which step would be affected first?
questions.context: In this simplified case, a male flower has pollen, a bee visits both kinds of flower, and a female flower has a swollen base. A visit alone does not promise fruit.

left.label: No pollen on the male flower
No insect moves between the two flowers
No ovary beneath the receiving petals

right.label: There is no donor material to transfer
The pollen lacks this route to the receiving flower
There is no fruit-forming structure at that flower

questions.explanation: Each missing element interrupts a different part of the path: supply, transfer, or a structure that could become fruit.

questions.prompt: A vine’s first blossoms have straight stems and fall away. Which note belongs in a garden journal?
questions.context: Illinois Extension says early flowers are commonly male; no swollen base was seen on these blossoms.

options.label: The observation fits early male flowers; keep watching later blossoms
The observation suggests a soil problem even though no female flowers were seen
The first later blossom with a swollen base will certainly make a fruit

questions.explanation: Male flowers do not have a developing fruit at their bases. This observation neither diagnoses the whole patch nor guarantees later fruit.

questions.prompt: A carver sets aside three parts of one cut pumpkin: outer rind, firm flesh, and the stringy central mass containing seeds. Which part matters for a later planting?
questions.context: This is a text description of the cut fruit; no diagram or ovals are displayed.

options.label: The outer rind because it protected this fruit
The firm flesh because it grew this season
The seeds in the central mass because they can grow into new plants

questions.explanation: The seed-bearing centre is the part that can start the next generation; rind and flesh belong to the present fruit.

questions.prompt: Two compatible varieties of the same Cucurbita species grew near each other. A gardener saved seeds from one fruit. Where might a cross become visible?
questions.context: Assume the pollen transfer occurred. Compare the already formed fruit with plants grown from its seeds.

options.label: In some plants grown from the saved seeds
As an immediate redesign of the fruit already on the vine
In every seedling with exactly the same new appearance

questions.explanation: Cross-pollination affects the genetic combination of seeds, so variation may appear in later plants; it does not redesign the current fruit.

questions.prompt: A fourth miniature at the shop has no variety tag. Which species label can you give it from size alone?
questions.context: Illinois Extension lists Jack-Be-Little as a C. pepo miniature, Big Max among C. maxima jumbos, and Dickinson Field among C. moschata processing pumpkins. These are named examples, not size rules.

options.label: None yet; the fourth miniature needs its own variety record
C. pepo, because Jack-Be-Little is miniature
C. maxima, because all shop pumpkins share the giant group

questions.explanation: The three named examples show that “pumpkin” spans species, but one miniature example cannot classify every other miniature.

questions.prompt: A visitor blames the neighbouring vine for this pumpkin’s yellow skin. Which reply combines the variety record with what you learned about crossing?
questions.context: Illinois Extension lists Big Autumn as yellow when mature. In this original case, a tagged Big Autumn fruit grew beside a different compatible variety.

options.label: The variety can mature yellow; crossing can show up in plants grown from its seeds.
The fruit has borrowed its neighbour’s colour; its saved seeds must remain unchanged.
Yellow proves this fruit is immature; compatible varieties cannot cross.

questions.explanation: Big Autumn supplies a named mature-yellow example. Compatible crossing changes the genetic combination in seeds, rather than repainting the current fruit. A colour change alone would not identify its pollen donor.

title: After the Flower: How Seeds Travel
description: Follow seeds through wings, digestion, forceful release and humidity-controlled cones. Separate release, travel, dormancy and population-level survival across eight discoveries.

sources.label: US Forest Service, Woody Plant Seed Manual, chapter 1
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, How plants hitchhike on animal poo
Original fictional case, choices and reasoning authored for this quiz.

note: Source-based mechanism questions and explicitly invented observation cards. A shape suggests a route but does not prove one seed’s path; a landed seed is not proof of germination. No flower-to-fruit reproduction or seed arithmetic.

questions.prompt: A small dry seed has a broad papery wing. Which journey does that shape make most plausible?
questions.context: Original observation card: the seed is dry, exposed and winged; no animal, fruit rupture or trip was observed.

options.label: A trip inside an animal after fleshy fruit is eaten
A trip aided by moving air
A trip propelled by a suddenly splitting fruit

questions.explanation: A wing increases the area available to moving air relative to the seed. The Forest Service describes wings on wind-dispersed woody seeds. A wing alone does not document this seed’s actual route.

questions.prompt: Which new observation would best distinguish stream transport from a wind-only story for one marked seed?
questions.context: Original field question: a winged marked seed was found on a bank after a windy day. Its trip was not witnessed; choose an observation to seek, not a claim that its wing determines the whole route.

options.label: A second similar seed appears on the bank
The marked seed has a pale coat
The marked seed is seen floating with the current

questions.explanation: Seeing the same marked seed afloat and moving with current directly documents a water leg. A similar seed or coat color cannot establish its route.

questions.prompt: A bird eats a fleshy fruit. Later, intact seeds appear in its droppings. Which feature best explains how this route can carry a seed?
questions.context: Original observation model: the bird swallowed seeds without chewing them, and intact seeds were found later. The route is observed in this model, but germination was not.

options.label: A protective seed coat can resist digestion
Brief transit makes every swallowed seed survive
The fleshy pulp stays intact and shields the seed throughout digestion

questions.explanation: Kew describes some swallowed seeds surviving passage because a protective coat resists digestion. Transit does not guarantee survival for every seed, and the pulp is digested.

questions.prompt: Put these shuffled cards into a possible forceful-release sequence.
questions.context: Original four-card model of one dry fruit. It gives the parts and events but no chronology. The sequence is conceptual and makes no claim about distance.

items.label: Seed comes to rest away from the fruit
Dry fruit wall tightens
Seed leaves the opened fruit
Fruit wall splits

questions.explanation: Drying can build tension; a sudden split ejects the seed, which later lands. The Forest Service names ceanothus and witch-hazel as examples, while Kew calls this ballistic dispersal.

questions.prompt: A loblolly pine cone opens in warm, dry air and closes as humidity rises. What does this change most directly regulate?
questions.context: Original observation based on the Forest Service account: loose seeds remain inside before the cone opens. No seedlings are being observed.

options.label: Whether a bird can digest every seed
Whether the seeds have already germinated
When seeds can leave the cone

questions.explanation: The Forest Service describes warm, dry opening and humid closing in loblolly pine cones. The moving scales regulate release; they are not a record of germination or digestive survival.

questions.prompt: Three seed lots have different delays. Which event is each note actually about?
questions.context: Original research summaries distinguish an unopened cone from a released, living seed. Classify the bottleneck, rather than assuming every delay is the same.

cells.label: Mature living seeds are still trapped behind closed cone scales
Seeds are already on the ground; an internal dormancy requirement has not yet been overcome
The fruit remains attached to its branch, retaining the seeds inside

questions.explanation: Retention and dormancy can both delay the next visible change, but at different stages. A living seed may be released yet remain dormant. These cases do not prescribe a species-specific treatment.

questions.prompt: A winged seed is recovered from bird droppings on a riverside path. Which account is best supported?
questions.context: Original card: the intact seed and the droppings were observed together; nobody saw the bird eat it or the seed germinate.

options.label: The wing proves it flew all the way to the path
Its present location proves it grew there
It survived an animal-carried leg, but its earlier and later route remains open

questions.explanation: The droppings support an ingestion route for this seed; its wing might support another possible leg, and a riverside location does not prove water travel or growth. Kew explains the animal mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why can a dispersal strategy be useful even when only a small fraction of its seeds become surviving seedlings?
questions.context: The question concerns populations and future habitat, not the fate of the individually marked seed in the earlier cards.

options.label: Its success depends on every transported seed landing in identical conditions
Transport can reach suitable sites even though many individual seeds never establish
Producing many seeds makes the later conditions for growth irrelevant

questions.explanation: The Forest Service describes large seed production with only a small fraction germinating and surviving; Kew explains transport to potentially more favourable environments. The opportunity to reach suitable sites matters without a guarantee for each seed.

title: Cold Surface Detective

Supercooled fog droplets struck the pane

Frozen dew after visible liquid beads

B: visible wet beads form, then freeze
C: fog droplets strike and freeze

The elevated air reading sets the minimum temperature for nearby surfaces
The exposed rail can cool below the air measured above it

Compare the coating’s shade with ice on a different surface

questions.context: Original final card: a fence has opaque white ice after fog, but no one saw it form; its surface temperature was not measured.

Frozen dew is proved because fog was present
White ice observed; droplet impact and surface temperature remain to be checked
