questions.context: The National Park Service explains that fossilization is uncommon and preservation depends on conditions. Rapid burial and hard parts can improve preservation chances, while many organisms and events leave no fossil record.
questions.explanation: Fossils preserve only some organisms and traces under particular conditions. Missing fossils do not prove that an organism or event never existed; the preserved record is incomplete and biased by preservation conditions.

options.label: Only some remains or traces are preserved, so the record is incomplete
Every organism is preserved equally and permanently
A trackway records every action the animal ever took

questions.prompt: Which pair of conditions can make preservation more likely, according to the NPS source?
questions.context: The National Park Service fossil-formation guide explains that preservation depends on both an organism’s remains and the conditions around them. It does not say any single condition guarantees a fossil.
questions.explanation: Rapid burial can protect remains from later damage, while hard parts tend to persist more readily than soft tissues. Both can improve the chance of preservation, but neither guarantees it.

options.label: Slow exposure and no durable remains
A record that includes every individual

questions.prompt: The fictional site preserves Morrowtail footprints and one limb bone, but no skin or color-bearing material. What can those clues establish about the animal’s skin color?
questions.context: The trackway and bone are invented examples of preserved evidence. The quiz provides no pigment, skin impression, or other color information.
questions.explanation: Footprints record activity and a limb bone preserves part of the body, but neither clue contains the missing skin-color information. The color remains unknown from this evidence.

options.label: The available clues do not establish skin color
The skin was definitely dark because the animal lived long ago
The trackway proves the skin matched the ground

title: Which Model Keeps the Ice Cold?
description: Compare fictional shelter scores, then test how an envelope, opening, moving air, and combined designs change the model result.

sections.title: Read one change at a time

sources.label: Original fictional shelter score table and rules; not measured data.

note: Every shelter, score, and result is an original fictional model, not a temperature or ice-mass measurement. Higher chill score means only that the supplied model held on to more pretend ice. The tasks do not test heat conduction through different materials.

questions.prompt: In this model, what does a higher chill score mean?
questions.context: Fictional score rule: shelters begin with the same pretend ice. A higher chill score means the model records more pretend ice still held by the shelter at the check. Scores are invented points, not degrees or grams.

options.label: The model held on to more pretend ice.
The room temperature was measured as lower.

questions.explanation: The rule defines the score as a model count of pretend ice held. It does not report a room temperature or a wind measurement.

questions.prompt: What does the matched pair of shelter runs support?
questions.context: Fictional run A used a thin envelope, closed flap, calm air, and scored 64. Run B used a padded envelope, the same closed flap and calm air, and scored 78. Both began with the same pretend-ice amount under the model rules.

options.label: The padded-envelope version scored higher in these two model runs.
A padded envelope always keeps real ice cold.

questions.explanation: Only the envelope description differs in this supplied pair, so the score comparison is about these model runs. It cannot establish an unrestricted result for real shelters.

questions.prompt: Match each model trial to the feature changed from its baseline.
questions.context: Each fictional trial starts at a baseline score of 64 with a thin envelope, a small closed flap, and calm air. Trial B has a padded envelope and scores 78. Trial C has a wide opening and scores 50. Trial D has a fan moving air and scores 56. Each trial changes only the named feature from the baseline.

left.label: Trial D: fan moving air, score 56

right.label: Air movement changed; score is lower.

questions.explanation: The model keeps the other listed conditions at baseline in each comparison. Matching the changed feature helps avoid crediting an opening or fan for the envelope trial's result.

questions.prompt: Compare each single-change score with the baseline score of 64.
questions.context: The fictional score table gives Trial B (padded envelope) 78, Trial C (wide opening) 50, and Trial D (fan moving air) 56. The baseline is 64. Use only these model scores.

cells.label: Trial B: 78
Trial C: 50
Trial D: 56

questions.explanation: The comparison is a simple check against the given baseline: 78 is above 64, while 50 and 56 are below it. These are fictional score differences, not measured temperature changes.

questions.prompt: Put the review steps in a useful order before comparing two combined designs.
questions.context: The fictional shelter table contains several designs with more than one feature changed. A fair reading starts by checking the shared starting conditions and ends by limiting the claim to the table.

items.label: Check that the listed starting conditions match.
Name the envelope, opening, and air features that differ.
Compare the two supplied scores.
State only what these model runs support.

questions.explanation: Checking the setup first helps show whether a score comparison is meaningful. Naming differences before comparing and then limiting the conclusion prevents the fictional table from being treated as a real-world guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which combined shelter scored higher in the supplied pair?
questions.context: Fictional combined run E used a padded envelope, a small closed flap, calm air, and scored 91. Run F used the same padded envelope and flap but had a fan moving air; it scored 70. The same pretend-ice starting rule applies to both.
questions.explanation: The displayed scores are 91 and 70, so E is higher. The pair differs in the stated air condition; it does not show that every fan or shelter behaves this way.

questions.prompt: A new fictional design must score at least 85. Which listed design meets that rule?
questions.context: In a separate fictional repeat with a newly prepared ice sample, the padded, small closed-flap design scores 89 in calm air and 72 with a fan. A thin-envelope baseline scores 64. This round’s target is 85 or more.
questions.explanation: Only 89 reaches the model's stated target of 85. The decision follows the fictional score rule, not an estimate of real shelter performance.

questions.prompt: Which summary stays within the evidence in this quiz?
questions.context: The shelter scores and designs in this quiz were invented as a self-contained comparison. No actual ice, temperature, shelter, or wind was measured.

options.label: One combined design scored higher in this fictional table; the table does not prove how every real shelter performs.
The table proves every padded shelter keeps ice cold in any weather.
The score is a measured room temperature in degrees.

questions.explanation: A conclusion should match what was recorded. The invented scores compare only the supplied model designs and are not temperature measurements or a universal result.

title: The Invisible Ocean Elevator
description: Use NOAA's explanation of density and sinking, then test isolated and combined changes in a clearly fictional ocean-water model.

sections.title: Test one model change at a time
Combine clues without shrinking the ocean

sources.label: NOAA National Ocean Service, Thermohaline Circulation
Original fictional density-index drawer and rules; not ocean measurements.

note: The drawer's scores are invented index points, not real density values. They isolate changes for practice and do not recreate or explain every route in the global ocean circulation.

questions.prompt: According to NOAA, which two properties control ocean-water density in the thermohaline explanation?
questions.context: NOAA explains that deep-ocean currents are driven by density differences and names the two properties in the term thermohaline.
questions.explanation: NOAA uses thermo for temperature and haline for salinity, and says both control ocean-water density in this explanation.

questions.prompt: In NOAA's polar example, why does surrounding seawater become saltier as sea ice forms?
questions.context: Use NOAA's stated account of sea ice forming in very cold ocean regions; choose the detail it gives about salt.

options.label: The salt is left behind in the surrounding seawater.
The salt turns into sea ice and leaves the water.
The wind adds new salt to the water.

questions.explanation: NOAA says that when sea ice forms, salt is left behind in the surrounding seawater; it does not describe wind adding salt.

questions.prompt: Order NOAA's short explanation for why some surrounding water sinks in this polar example.
questions.context: Use the sequence stated on NOAA's Thermohaline Circulation page. The task asks for that described chain, not a complete map of ocean currents.

items.label: Sea ice forms in very cold regions.
Salt is left in the surrounding seawater.
The surrounding seawater becomes saltier.
That seawater becomes denser.
The denser seawater starts to sink.

questions.explanation: NOAA links sea-ice formation to salt remaining in the surrounding water, then to higher salinity, higher density, and sinking. This is one described process, not the whole conveyor route.

questions.prompt: What changed in the cooled-cell comparison?
questions.context: Original fictional drawer: identical cells start at index 50. In the cooled-only cell, the temperature setting is lower while the salinity setting stays the same; its invented density index is 54. The index has no real units.

options.label: Only the temperature setting changed; the fictional index rose from 50 to 54.
Only the salinity setting changed; the index fell to 46.
Both settings changed, so the comparison cannot isolate either one.

questions.explanation: The context holds salinity steady and changes only the temperature setting, so this fictional pair isolates that setting. Its index values are not real density measurements.

questions.prompt: Match each isolated fictional trial to its difference from the reference index of 50.
questions.context: The original drawer keeps all unlisted settings at the reference. Cooled only: 54. Freshened only: 48. Saltier only: 53. These invented index points are for comparing the supplied cases, not for measuring seawater.
questions.explanation: Subtracting the shared reference of 50 gives +4, −2, and +3. Because the drawer is fictional, those differences describe its index only.

questions.prompt: Mark each isolated trial as above or below the reference index of 50.
questions.context: All values belong to the original fictional drawer: cooled only = 54; warmed only = 46; freshened only = 48; saltier only = 53. The values are invented index points.

cells.label: Cooled only: 54
Warmed only: 46
Freshened only: 48
Saltier only: 53

questions.explanation: Each row compares its displayed number with 50. The result is arithmetic on a fictional index, not a claim about the size of real ocean-density changes.

questions.prompt: Which combined fictional cell has the higher index?
questions.context: The original model drawer reports warm plus fresh = 43 and cool plus salty = 59. Both are invented index points from the same fictional comparison.
questions.explanation: 59 is greater than 43 in the supplied model. This combined result does not show that separate changes always add in a simple way; the task uses only the given combined scores.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion uses both the NOAA source and the fictional drawer carefully?
questions.context: NOAA describes deep-ocean currents as driven by density differences controlled by temperature and salinity. The drawer contains only a few invented cells and index points; it has no ocean map or current route.

options.label: The drawer helps compare its stated cases, while NOAA's ocean circulation is broader than this small model.
Every ocean current is caused only by the two-cell changes in this drawer.
The drawer identifies the route and speed of the global conveyor.

questions.explanation: NOAA supports the density connection in its circulation explanation, but the invented drawer gives no basin map, route, or speed. A small model comparison cannot supply those missing details.

title: Check the Claim About the Vanishing Ice
description: Audit fictional closed-jar and open-tray records, separating a changed label or reading from a claim the record cannot prove.

sources.label: Original fictional mass-record ledger and rules; not a physical experiment.

note: The jars, trays, labels, and mass units are original fictional records. Conclusions apply only to what each record says; the quiz gives no instructions for a household experiment.

questions.prompt: What changed in the sealed-jar record?
questions.context: Fictional ledger: the whole sealed jar and its contents read 150 model mass units at the first check, labeled “liquid.” At the second check, the whole sealed jar again reads 150 units, labeled “ice.” The labels are the ledger's supplied descriptions.

options.label: The whole-jar reading stayed 150; the ledger's appearance label changed.
The jar lost 6 units between checks.
The ledger measured the room around the jar.

questions.explanation: Both listed whole-jar readings are 150. The descriptive label differs, but the ledger does not report a change in the whole-jar reading.

questions.prompt: What does the open-tray ledger show?
questions.context: In a separate fictional record, an open tray's visible-content reading is 20 model mass units at the first check and 14 units at the later check. No other nearby surface or container is included in either reading.

options.label: The recorded open-tray reading is 6 units lower at the later check.
The ledger found the other 6 units on a nearby surface.
The two tray readings are equal.

questions.explanation: 20 minus 14 is 6, so the later tray reading is lower by 6 model units. Because nearby places were not measured, this record does not locate that difference.

questions.prompt: Match each fictional ledger entry to the statement it supports.
questions.context: The ledger's boundary rule: a reading covers only the named object or contents listed for that row. A blank nearby-location column means no reading was recorded there.

right.label: The listed whole-jar readings are equal.
The listed tray reading is 6 units lower later.

questions.explanation: Each row supports a statement about exactly the object and time recorded. A blank location is missing evidence, not a measurement of what happened there.

questions.prompt: Mark each statement as supported or not supported by the fictional ledger.
questions.context: The sealed jar reads 150 units at both checks. The open tray's reading changes from 20 to 14 units. No nearby place is measured, and no other record is supplied.

cells.label: The two whole-jar readings match.
The later tray reading is 6 units lower.
A nearby surface received exactly 6 units.
The ledger proves the recorded amount vanished.

questions.explanation: The first two statements repeat what the records show. The last two go beyond the measurement boundary because no surrounding location or complete system is recorded.

questions.prompt: Why can't the open-tray record say where the reading difference went?
questions.context: The fictional tray log measures only the tray's visible contents at two times. Its surrounding table, air, and any other container are outside the named record.

options.label: The log does not measure the surrounding places, so it cannot identify a destination.
The record proves the difference moved into the air.
The record proves all of the contents became ice.

questions.explanation: A reading limited to the tray cannot establish what happened outside that boundary. The other options name destinations or changes that the fictional log never measured.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for checking a new mass-record claim.
questions.context: This is a reasoning routine for the original fictional ledger, not a procedure for conducting an experiment.

items.label: Identify exactly what the record includes.
Compare the displayed readings at the listed times.
Keep a description label separate from a mass reading.
State only the conclusion supported by those records.

questions.explanation: A claim can be checked only after its measurement boundary is clear. Then the readings and labels can be separated before drawing a limited conclusion.

questions.prompt: A new fictional jar has two equal whole-container readings but different appearance labels. Which statement follows?
questions.context: Transfer case in the original model: jar R reads 90 model mass units at both checks. Its supplied labels are “liquid” and later “ice.” No claim about any unmeasured object is included.

options.label: The supplied whole-container readings are equal; the labels describe the recorded appearance.
This case proves that every real container always has the same mass.
The record shows that 90 units moved to a nearby object.

questions.explanation: The only numeric evidence is 90 at both checks for the whole fictional jar. The labels do not add a measurement of another object or establish a universal physical rule.

questions.prompt: Which headline is the most careful description of the open-tray record?
questions.context: The fictional open tray reads 20 model units and later 14. The log leaves all surrounding locations unmeasured.

options.label: The tray's recorded reading changed; the log does not track the surrounding places.
Six units vanished from every part of the system.
The log found six units on the table.

questions.explanation: The careful headline reports the lower tray reading and also names the missing measurement boundary. The other headlines turn an unmeasured possibility into a fact.

title: What Changed Behind the Beaver Dam?
description: Read a fictional site record about changes in water depth, ponding, and a wet floodplain hollow, then compare a separate site without drawing broad flood claims.

sections.title: Read the Willow Bend record
sections.description: Separate mapped observations from claims the record cannot support.

sections.title: Compare without overreaching
sections.description: Transfer the reasoning to a separate site and note what remains unknown.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a direct report from the later Willow Bend record?
questions.explanation: The fictional paired record reports a higher depth mark at point A and a larger mapped ponded area. It contains no downstream flood or removal evidence.
questions.context: Fictional Willow Bend notes. At the upstream marker A, water reads 12 cm on the first visit and 20 cm on the second. The same map squares show a ponded area growing from three squares to five.

options.label: The downstream town had less flooding.
The marked upstream depth is higher and the mapped pond is larger.
The dam stopped every floodplain from getting wet.
Removing the dam would restore the first map.

questions.prompt: Match each Willow Bend record detail to the change it describes.
questions.explanation: The depth mark describes local water depth; the wet side hollow shows water over a low floodplain area; the larger area behind the structure describes ponding.
questions.context: At fictional Willow Bend, observers recorded a higher upstream mark, water filling a side hollow on the floodplain, and a larger mapped pond behind the dam. USGS has examined how beaver dams can alter water depth and spread water into low areas.

left.label: Water in the shallow side hollow

right.label: Greater depth at the marked point
Floodplain area has water on the later visit

questions.prompt: Choose the best reading of each map note.
questions.explanation: The photo shows water around the low marker and a dry bench upslope. It does not show what happened downstream or at other dams.
questions.context: Fictional paired photos. On the second visit, a trail marker in a low side hollow is surrounded by water. A bench farther upslope is dry. The photos cover the hollow and the bench only.

cells.label: Water surrounds the low marker on the second visit.
The bench upslope is dry in the second-visit photo.
The dam prevented a downstream flood.
Every beaver dam creates the same map change.

questions.prompt: How could the pool and the trickle be present at the same time?
questions.explanation: A dam can hold back some water and allow some to pass. The pool and the trickle do not require the dam to be watertight.
questions.context: USGS describes how a semi-porous beaver dam can hold water behind it. At a fictional second dam, an upstream pool and a narrow trickle flowing out through part of the dam are visible at the same time.

options.label: The pool proves the dam blocks all flow.
The dam holds back some water while letting some pass.
The trickle proves the pool cannot contain water.
The dam guarantees the same flow at every point.

questions.prompt: Match each Cedar Bend observation to what it can support.
questions.explanation: Cedar Bend has ponding on both maps and the same point-A depth reading. Willow Bend’s depth change belongs to its own fictional record, not Cedar Bend.
questions.context: At fictional Cedar Bend, maps depict a pool upstream on both visits. A marked stake reads 14 cm each time. At a different site, Willow Bend’s later depth mark was higher.

left.label: A ponded area appears on both maps
Point A reads 14 cm on both visits
Willow Bend had a higher later depth mark

right.label: Ponding is shown on both Cedar Bend visits
No change in the recorded depth at this point
A result from a different fictional site

questions.prompt: Which added record would best help check whether different weather could explain a map change?
questions.explanation: Rainfall and upstream flow records would test whether water arriving at the site differed. They would not, by themselves, isolate the dam’s effect.
questions.context: A larger pool appears on the second fictional Willow Bend visit, after the same dam has been there for both visits. The water level could also have responded to weather. The two readings were taken weeks apart.

options.label: Rainfall and upstream flow records around each visit.
A drawing of an unrelated dam at another river.
A list of beaver names from a wildlife poster.
A downstream flood claim without a date or measurement.

questions.prompt: For each proposed conclusion, mark whether the supplied records support it.
questions.explanation: The marked Willow Bend point rose, while Cedar Bend’s point stayed the same and both Cedar Bend maps show ponding. Neither site record establishes that a downstream neighborhood was protected.
questions.context: Fictional comparison. Willow Bend’s marked point rose from 12 to 20 cm. Cedar Bend’s marked point stayed at 14 cm, and a ponded area appears on both Cedar Bend maps.

cells.label: Cedar Bend’s point-A readings are equal on the two visits.
The two sites show an identical depth change.
Cedar Bend’s maps show a ponded area on both visits.
A downstream neighborhood was protected from a flood.

questions.prompt: What remains unknown from these fictional maps?
questions.explanation: The records state Willow Bend’s higher later mark and Cedar Bend’s equal readings and ponded areas. They include no downstream gauge or flood record, so no downstream flood conclusion follows.
questions.context: A fictional town sits downstream from Willow Bend. The upstream maps show how far the pool extends near the dam. No town readings or observations during storms appear on those maps.

options.label: Whether the two named sites have any ponded area at all.
Whether a downstream flood happened or whether a dam prevented one.
Whether Willow Bend’s later point-A mark is higher.
Whether Cedar Bend’s point-A readings match.

sources.label: USGS, “Hydraulic Effects of Beaver Dams” (flow, depth, ponding, and floodplain inundation)
Original fictional beaver-dam site maps and observation records.
